title: Anise Biscotti
changes_from_base: Crushed anise seeds and lemon zest replace the orange zest; fewer almonds (100 g).
summary: These anise biscotti follow the classic almond biscotti method, with lightly crushed anise seeds and lemon zest replacing the orange zest and fewer almonds for a lighter, more aniseed-forward bite.
equipment: large metal baking tray lined with baking paper

ingredients.item: fine sea salt or table salt
whole blanched almonds, toasted and roughly chopped

steps.title: Heat the oven
steps.text: Set the oven to 175°C (155°C fan) and let it heat for at least 20 minutes, with a shelf in the middle. This recipe uses the same two-bake method as the classic almond biscotti, but swaps in crushed anise seeds and lemon zest for the orange zest, with fewer almonds.

steps.title: Whisk eggs and flavourings
steps.text: Whisk the eggs, caster sugar, vanilla and salt together for about a minute until smooth and lightly frothy, then stir in the crushed anise seeds and lemon zest before whisking in the cooled melted butter. Adding the seeds and zest directly to the egg mixture lets their oils spread evenly through the dough rather than staying clumped in one spot. You should be able to smell the anise as soon as it goes in.

steps.title: Bring in the dry ingredients
steps.text: Stir in the flour and baking powder until a soft, sticky dough forms, then fold through the chopped almonds. Mix only until combined, since overworking the dough at this stage can leave the baked biscotti dense rather than light. The dough should look flecked with lemon zest and crushed seeds throughout.

steps.title: Shape two logs
steps.text: With damp hands, shape the dough into two logs on the lined tray, each about 25 x 6 cm and 2 cm high, spaced about 8 cm apart. Wet hands keep the sticky dough from pulling apart as you shape it. Leave the gap between the logs, as they will widen during baking.

steps.title: First bake
steps.text: Bake for 25-30 minutes, until the logs are golden, firm on top and just starting to crack. The surface cracks are a useful signal that the dough has set enough to hold together when sliced. Give the full time rather than checking too early, since the centre needs to firm up along with the crust.

steps.title: Cool before slicing
steps.text: Let the logs cool on the tray for 20-25 minutes before cutting into them. Slicing too soon crumbles the warm crumb, while waiting until fully cold makes the log brittle enough to shatter under the knife. This middle stage, firm but not hard, gives the cleanest slices.

steps.title: Lower the oven and slice
steps.text: Turn the oven down to 150°C (130°C fan). On a board, cut each log on the diagonal into 1.5 cm slices with a serrated knife, using a gentle sawing motion rather than pushing straight down. Sawing gently keeps the almond pieces intact instead of tearing the slice apart.

steps.title: Second bake to dry out
steps.text: Stand or lay the slices back on the tray and bake for 20-25 minutes, turning once, until they are dry and lightly golden at the cut edges. This lower, longer bake is what dries the crumb out for a proper crunch, rather than browning it further. The anise aroma becomes noticeably stronger as the slices dry.

steps.title: Cool completely
steps.text: Transfer to a wire rack and leave to cool fully before storing. The biscotti crisp up considerably as they cool, so don't judge their final texture until they're completely cold. Makes about 30 biscotti.

tips: Crush the anise seeds lightly with the back of a spoon or a pestle and mortar before adding them — whole seeds release less flavour and can feel gritty in the finished biscuit.
Add the lemon zest and anise seeds to the egg mixture early, so their oils disperse through the whole batch rather than settling in pockets.
Don't slice the logs straight from the oven — a common mistake that crumbles the warm crumb; give them the full 20-25 minute rest first.
Use a gentle sawing action with a serrated knife so the almond pieces don't tear the slice as you cut.
If you want a stronger anise flavour, crush the seeds a little finer, but avoid grinding them to a powder or the flavour can turn bitter.
safety: Don't taste the raw dough or batter: raw flour and raw egg aren't safe to eat until baked.
storage: Store in an airtight tin at room temperature for up to 2 weeks. They freeze well for up to 3 months; thaw at room temperature before serving.
